title: Basic sentence order (A1)
explanation: Basic Chinese sentence structure. Subject‑verb and subject‑verb‑object. Simple sentences are similar to English; complex sentences differ in word order for time, location and adverbs.

title: Time words and word order (A2)
structure: Time + Subj. + Verb + Obj.；Subj. + Time + Verb + Obj.
explanation: Time expressions can go either at the start of sentence or right after subject. Do NOT put time words at sentence‑end.

examples.en: Yesterday I went to the bar.
I went to the bar yesterday.

examples.pinyin: Xià gè xīngqī tā yào huí guó.
examples.en: Next week he is going back to his country.

examples.pinyin: Tā xià gè xīngqī yào huí guó.
examples.en: He is going back to his country next week.

title: Indicating location with "zai" before verbs (A2)
explanation: In Chinese, location phrase 在+地点 must come before the verb, unlike English which puts location after verb.

examples.en: I go to college in Shanghai.

examples.pinyin: Bù yào zài chuáng shàng chī dōngxi.
examples.en: Don't eat food on the bed.

examples.zh: 很多人在地铁上吃早饭。
examples.pinyin: Hěn duō rén zài dìtiě shàng chī zǎofàn.
examples.en: Many people eat breakfast on the subway.
The boss is seeing the client in the meeting room.

similar: Expressing existence in a place with "zai" (A1)

title: The "also" adverb "ye" (A1)
structure: Subj. + 也 + Verb / Verb Phrase；Subj. + 也 (+ Adv.) + Adj.
explanation: Adverb 也 means also / too / either. Always placed before verb/adjective, never at sentence end. In negative sentences still use 也 before negation.

title: Simple "noun + adjective" sentences (A1)
explanation: Adjective predicates use 很 before adjective, NOT 是. Sometimes 很 is only grammatical filler, not meaning "very".

title: Tag questions with "ma" (A1)
structure: ⋯⋯，好 / 对 / 是 / 可以 + 吗？
explanation: Add 吗 at sentence‑end for confirmation questions meaning right? / OK?.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen qù nǐ jiā, hǎo ma?
examples.en: Let's go to your place, OK?

examples.pinyin: Nǐ méi lái guo, shì ma?

examples.zh: 我现在想去洗手间，可以吗？
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiànzài xiǎng qù xǐshǒujiān, kěyǐ ma?
examples.en: I want to go to the bathroom now. Is that OK?

title: Questions with "ne" (A1)
structure: Topic + 呢？；[Missing Person / Thing] + 呢？
explanation: Particle 呢 for "what about…?". Can also ask where something/someone is when context is clear.

examples.en: This one is good. What about that one?

title: Placement of question words (A1)
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么 + (Noun)？；Subj. + Verb + 哪里 / 哪儿？；Subj. + 是 + 谁？；Subj. + 什么时候 + Predicate？；Subj. + 为什么 + Predicate？；Subj. + 怎么 + Verb (+ Obj.)？
explanation: Chinese wh‑question words stay in the same position as the answer, do NOT move to sentence front like English.

title: Expressing possession with "de" (A1)
explanation: Particle 的 marks possession, similar to English apostrophe‑s. Noun1’s Noun2.

title: Expressing possession with "you" (A1)
explanation: Verb 有 means “to have”. Negate with 没有, cannot use 不有.

examples.en: I don't have a cell phone.

title: Standard negation with "bu" (A1)
structure: Subj. + 不 + Verb + Obj.；Subj. + 不 + Adj.
explanation: 不 negates verbs and adjectives for present / future / habitual situations. Exception: cannot negate verb 有 with 不, use 没有.

title: Negation of "you" with "mei" (A1)
explanation: Negate verb 有 with 没有. Short form 没 is allowed. Never say 不有.

examples.en: Does he not have a job?

title: Connecting nouns with "shi" (A1)
explanation: 是 links noun to noun, meaning “to be”. Cannot link noun‑adjective pairs; use 很 for adjectives.

title: Expressing existence in a place with "zai" (A1)
explanation: Verb 在 means to be in / at a location. Do not add verb 是.
similar: Expressing location with "zai... shang / xia / li" (A2)

title: Expressing existence with "you" (A1)
explanation: Pattern Place + 有 expresses “there is / there are”, location has something.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu hěn duō xiǎo gǒu.
examples.en: There are a lot of puppies in my home.
Is there any water in the cup?
Is there anyone in the room?

title: Using the verb "jiao" (A1)
explanation: Verb 叫 means “to be called / named”.

examples.en: This place is called the Bund.

title: Using the verb "qu" (A1)
explanation: Verb 去 means go. Directly connect place after 去; no preposition equivalent of English "to". Can also be followed by verb meaning go‑to‑do‑something.

examples.en: In the afternoon, I'll go to the supermarket.
Would you like to go travel?

title: The "all" adverb "dou" (A1)
explanation: Adverb 都 means all / both / neither. Must be placed after subject and before verb, not sentence‑beginning.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen liǎng gè dōu ài nǐ.
examples.en: The two of us both love you.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé wǒ tàitai dōu bù chī ròu.
examples.en: Neither my wife nor I eat meat.

title: Expressing "excessively" with "tai" (A1)
explanation: 太……了 means too / so, can express complaint or exclamation.

title: Expressing "and" with "he" (A1)
explanation: 和 connects nouns only. Do NOT connect verbs or whole sentences with 和.

examples.en: The boss likes coffee and tea.

examples.pinyin: Shǒujī hé diànnǎo dōu hěn guì.
examples.en: Cell phones and computers are both expensive.

examples.pinyin: Yéye hé nǎinai dōu qīshí suì.
examples.en: My grandpa and grandma are both seventy years old.

title: Offering choices with "haishi" (A1)
structure: Option A + 还是 + Option B？；Subj. + Verb + Option A + 还是 + Option B？
explanation: 还是 used for “or” inside questions, to present two alternatives. Not for declarative‑sentence “or”.

examples.pinyin: Là de háishì bù là de?
Nǐ yào hē chá háishì kāfēi?
examples.en: Do you want to drink tea or coffee?

examples.zh: 他是美国人还是英国人？
examples.pinyin: Tā shì Měiguó rén háishì Yīngguó rén?

title: Structure of numbers (A1)
explanation: Rules for reading Chinese numbers from 1‑9999. Phone numbers read digit‑by‑digit; one pronounced yāo for phone numbers to avoid confusion with seven qī.

title: Structure of times (basic) (A1)
structure: (Date / Day) + x 点；x 点 + 半
explanation: Tell time: hour + 点 for o’clock. 半 for half‑past. Use 上午 / 下午 for a.m./p.m. Two o’clock uses 两点 not 二点.
similar: Structure of days of the week (A1)

title: Structure of days of the week (A1)
structure: 星期 + Number；星期天 / 星期日
explanation: Monday=星期一 … Saturday=星期六; Sunday=星期天 / 星期日. In Chinese calendar week starts on Monday.

examples.zh: 星期六和星期天我们不上班。
examples.pinyin: Xīngqīliù hé Xīngqītiān wǒmen bù shàngbān.
examples.en: Saturday and Sunday we don't work.

examples.zh: 下个星期四是我的生日。
examples.pinyin: Xià gè Xīngqīsì shì wǒ de shēngrì.

examples.en: I'm not here in Shanghai on Wednesday.

title: Structure of dates (A1)
structure: x 年 + y 月 + z 日；x 年 + y 月 + z 号
explanation: Big‑to‑small order: year‑month‑day. Spoken: 号; written/formal: 日.

examples.pinyin: Shí‑èryuè èrshí‑sì rì shì Píng'ān Yè.
Shíyuè yī hào wǒmen qù Shànghǎi.
examples.en: We will go to Shanghai on October 1st.

similar: Structure of days of the week (A1)

title: Measure word "ge" (A1)
structure: Number + 个 + Noun；Verb + 个 + Noun
explanation: 个 is the most common measure‑word classifier. Can be used as fallback when forgetting more specific measure‑words. Number one can omit to mean “a / an”.
